sections.heading: 0 Course Structure and Time Allocation
points: Hey there! Let's get our bearings first. The course is broken down into four clear chunks: Part I takes 12 hours, Part II.1 takes 12 hours, Part II.2 takes 6 hours, and Part III wraps up with 6 hours. Anything flagged with a star (⋆) or sitting in Section 4 is reserved for the Advanced Mathematics track, so you can breathe easy knowing those parts are not required for regular exams.

Here is how testing is organized across the semester. We kick off on February 9, 2026, with an 8-question multiple-choice quiz on Evalmee lasting 30 minutes, covering Exercises 1 through 17. Next comes a 60-minute paper exam on March 9, 2026, covering all non-starred exercises. Finally, there is a comprehensive 90-minute written exam in June 2026 that also covers all non-starred material. Take a moment to reflect: how can pacing yourself through the non-starred core exercises each week save you from last-minute stress before March?

sections.heading: 1 Determinant
points: We build determinants from the ground up using permutations in the symmetric group S_n, which contains all n! bijections of the set of integers from 1 to n. Any permutation breaks down into cycles and transpositions (which just swap two elements). Its signature is defined as (-1)^p, where p counts those transpositions. Using this, the determinant of an n-by-n matrix A sums over all permutations the product of entries times the permutation's signature. For example, in Exercise 1, we write out S_1, S_2, and S_3, and see how a 2-by-2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] simply works out to ad - bc.

Determinants act as the ultimate test for linear independence, invertibility, and geometric scaling. If det(A) is non-zero, the matrix is invertible, its column vectors form a basis, and a system like Ax = b has a unique solution. For instance, in Exercise 4, computing the determinant of a 3-by-3 matrix directly gives the volume of the parallelepiped formed by its columns. In Exercise 7, setting det(A) != 0 gives the exact conditions on a parameter m for invertibility. Determinants also unlock discrete patterns: in Exercise 11, the determinant of a power of [[1, 1], [1, 0]] neatly proves Cassini's identity for Fibonacci numbers, F_{n+1}F_{n-1} - F_n^2 = (-1)^n. How does picturing determinant as an area or volume help you instantly see why a zero determinant means the matrix collapses space?

sections.heading: 2 Exercises on Endomorphism Reduction
points: Section 2.1 focuses on the practical mechanics of diagonalizing a matrix into M = P D P^(-1). We look for eigenvalues (roots of the characteristic polynomial) and their matching eigenvectors to construct our invertible change-of-basis matrix P and diagonal matrix D. In Exercise 12, we practice this speed-run style on 2-by-2 and 3-by-3 matrices like M_1 = [[0, 1], [-2, 3]]. In Exercise 14, we see that diagonalizability can be spotted from several angles at once: factoring the characteristic polynomial, checking matrix rank, or noticing polynomial relations like A^2. We also see that when a matrix fails to be diagonalizable—like matrix C in Exercise 17—the Cayley-Hamilton theorem gives us an annihilating polynomial that still lets us compute powers C^n and invert C efficiently.

Section 2.2 puts these tools to work on real-world systems. In Exercise 24, a predator-prey model tracks antelopes (a_n) and lions (l_n) over time via U_{n+1} = A U_n. By finding eigenvalues and diagonalizing A = P D P^(-1), we compute A^n effortlessly, letting us determine the exact long-term survival of both populations as n approaches infinity. We also explore the matrix exponential exp(M) = sum M^k / k! in Exercise 26, discovering that det(exp(M)) = exp(tr(M)). Exercise 27 introduces stochastic matrices whose rows sum to 1, showing that 1 is always an eigenvalue and powers M^n remain stochastic. Why is turning a messy coupled system into decoupled diagonal coordinates such a game-changer for predicting the distant future?

sections.heading: 3 Theoretical Exercises
points: This theoretical section unites everything we know about diagonalizability. Exercise 28 proves the core equivalence: a matrix A is diagonalizable over R if and only if its characteristic polynomial splits with algebraic multiplicity equal to geometric multiplicity for every eigenvalue, which is equivalent to R^n splitting into a direct sum of eigenspaces. Exercise 29 and 30 nail down crucial spectral truths: the trace is the sum of eigenvalues, the determinant is the product of eigenvalues, and 0 belongs to the spectrum if and only if the matrix is non-invertible. For example, if Sp(A) = {0, 1, 2}, its determinant is immediately 0, meaning it cannot be inverted.

We also explore structural families of matrices. Exercise 31 proves similarity (A = P B P^(-1)) is an equivalence relation that preserves determinants, traces, rank, characteristic polynomials, and spectra. Exercise 33 unpacks projection matrices satisfying P^2 = P, showing their eigenvalues can only ever be 0 or 1, decomposing space cleanly into ker(P) direct sum Im(P). Exercise 34 examines nilpotent matrices, where M^p = 0; their only eigenvalue is 0, their trace and determinant are both 0, and their nilpotency index never exceeds n. What everyday actions around you behave like a projection—leaving things completely unchanged once applied a second time?

sections.heading: 4 Optional Exercises
points: The optional advanced track ventures into specialized linear algebra gems. Exercise 35 investigates the Vandermonde matrix V(alpha_1, ..., alpha_n), using polynomial roots to factorize its determinant into a product of differences (alpha_j - alpha_i). Exercises 36 and 37 look at limits of powers lim A^n = B and matrices whose spectra consist purely of integers.

Finally, Exercises 38 and 39 bridge into modern algorithms and advanced algebra. Exercise 38 models web navigation using Google's PageRank, where a directed graph's stochastic transition matrix and a damping factor alpha guarantee a unique stationary vector. Exercise 39 formalizes the minimal polynomial mu_A—the monic annihilating polynomial of lowest degree. It divides the characteristic polynomial, shares the exact same roots (the spectrum), and reveals that A is diagonalizable if and only if mu_A splits into distinct linear factors. Reflect on this: how does adding a tiny random jump factor alpha in PageRank prevent a random surfer from getting stuck in an infinite loop on the web?

key_terms.definition: A bijection from the finite set [[1, n]] onto itself, with the set of all such bijections forming the symmetric group S_n of size n!. Analogy: Think of it like a game of musical chairs where every single player must switch to a chair; everyone ends up seated, but in a rearranged order.

A 2-cycle permutation that swaps exactly two elements while leaving every other element fixed. Analogy: Think of two people trading seats in a movie theater while nobody else in the row moves an inch.

The number (-1)^p, where p is the total number of transpositions needed to produce the permutation. Analogy: Think of a standard two-way light switch: flipping it any odd number of times leaves the light in a different state, while any even number of flips returns it to where it started.

A scalar calculated from a square matrix by summing over all permutations the signed product of chosen entries, indicating invertibility when non-zero. Analogy: Think of an inflatable balloon's volume gauge: if the scale factor drops to zero, the whole shape has been crushed flat into zero volume and cannot be blown back out.

A square matrix M that can be written in the form PDP^(-1), where D is a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues and P is an invertible matrix of eigenvectors. Analogy: Think of adjusting your perspective or untangling messy crossed puppet strings so that each string pulls purely in one single independent direction without interfering with the others.

A polynomial P such that plugging in the matrix yields the zero matrix, P(M) = 0. Analogy: Think of a master reset combination on an electronic keypad that completely clears the screen back to total zero.

A square matrix with non-negative entries between 0 and 1 whose entries along each row sum up to exactly 1. Analogy: Think of a restaurant menu where each row represents a customer's total budget of 100%, divided up entirely among different courses.

Two square matrices A and B for which there exists an invertible matrix P such that A = P B P^(-1). Analogy: Think of describing the exact same musical tune in two different musical keys; the notes look completely different on the page, but the melody and harmonies are identical.

A matrix P satisfying the identity P^2 = P, sending any vector onto its image along its kernel. Analogy: Think of casting a silhouette on a wall: once an object casts its flat shadow, shining the light a second time on that shadow changes nothing at all.

A matrix M for which some positive power equals the zero matrix, M^p = 0. Analogy: Think of an echo bouncing down a canyon that completely dies out into absolute silence after a fixed number of bounces.

The unique monic polynomial of smallest possible degree that annihilates the matrix A. Analogy: Think of the absolute shortest, most concise instruction manual that tells you the exact cycle needed to return a machine to factory default.
